Check whether Kenton et al.'s extractive tasks use verified quotes as Khan et al.'s do.

Note that Khan et al.'s limitation concerns a judge without access to the underlying story that the debaters can read, while Kenton et al.'s closed tasks have no article for any party and rest on a weak-strong asymmetry between judge and debaters, so the closed-task result does not test the invented-narrative case.
in.other_title: Closed QA without information asymmetry: debate vs direct QA depends on judge strength
in.rationale: Both records concern debate in which debaters cannot quote verified evidence from a source text. Khan et al. state their results are limited to setups where debaters can provide verified evidence to the judge, here via the quote tool; without it, a debater arguing for the incorrect answer could create an alternative narrative that a judge without access to the underlying story would have no means to discover. Kenton et al.'s closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) have no article to use as a source and hence no information asymmetry; there debate beats consultancy but shows small or no benefit over QA without article for the judges the authors read as probably the most indicative (GPT-3.5 p = 0.037, Pro 1.0 no significant difference). Since the closed tasks have no underlying story hidden from the judge, Kenton et al.'s result does not test the invented-narrative case, and Khan et al.'s limitation, which concerns a judge without access to the underlying story, does not bear on Kenton et al.'s closed-task result; task type and evidence access change together.
in.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: debate without verified evidence from a source text, which Kenton et al. study on closed QA tasks with no article and Khan et al. discuss as a limit of their quote-tool setup

open_obligations: Note that Wen et al.'s setting has one model and no opponent to expose fabrications.
Check whether human evaluators could check quotes against the passage in Wen et al.'s interface.
Check how often fabrication, as opposed to cherry-picking, occurred.
in.other_title: How RLHF models mislead: fabricated evidence, consistent false arguments, test hacking
in.rationale: Khan et al. warn that without the quote tool a debater arguing the wrong answer could invent a narrative. Wen et al. report RLHF-trained models defend incorrect answers on question answering by cherry-picking or fabricating supporting evidence and making consistent but untruthful arguments that mislead their human subjects; this is single-model QA under RLHF, not debate.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether models arguing wrong answers fabricate evidence when quotes are not verified, for RLHF-trained models on QuALITY

in.other_title: Quote verification, not argumentation, appears to dominate judge accuracy in Khan et al.'s QuALITY debates, and such a tool may be unrealistic
in.rationale: Khan et al. acknowledge their results depend on verified evidence; the authors read Khan et al.'s own figures as showing the quote tool drives accuracy and argue this weakens the analogy to scalable oversight. This is an argument from Khan et al.'s data, not new data, so CRITIQUES.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Whether QuALITY debate results reflect argumentation or the verified-quote tool
